kzz7yh-f124277-d1e103.summary: Announces two questions on the first topic, the power of sinning.

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e108.summary: First question: whether the power of sinning is any power at all.

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e113.summary: Second question: whether the power of sinning is from God.

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e119.summary: First argument that the power to sin is not a power: Anselm says the power to sin is neither freedom nor part of freedom, but any such power would have to be one or the other.
claims: The power to sin is neither freedom nor a part of it (Anselm).

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e135.summary: Second argument: Anselm says a will unable to desert rectitude is freer than one able to; if the power to sin were a real power, it would make the will more powerful and nobler, not less free.
claims: A will that cannot sin is freer (Anselm).

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e155.summary: Third argument: being able to fail bodily (to die) is not a power, so a fortiori being able to fail spiritually (to sin) is not.
claims: Capacity to fail is not a power (argument).

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e162.summary: Sed contra from Augustine's Retractations: the will is that by which we sin and live rightly, and the will is a power.
claims: The will is the power by which one sins.

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e172.summary: Second sed contra: knowing how to sin is knowing and willing to sin is willing, so being able to sin is being able.
claims: By parity, posse peccare is a posse (argument).

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e179.summary: Richard's solution: the power of sinning is a defectible power. Defectibility diminishes the notion of power, so in respect of its defectibility it is not power but rather impotence, while in respect of the essence to which the defectibility is attached it is a power.
claims: The power to sin is a defectible power.
As defectible it is rather impotence; in its essence it is a power.

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e192.summary: The arguments that it is not a power hold of it in respect of the defectibility by which its act fails, the failure being the deformity of the sinful act.
claims: The deformity of sin arises from the will's defectibility.

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e201.summary: Reply to Augustine's argument: asking whether the will is a power differs from asking whether the power to sin is one, though they are the same thing. 'Will' does not include defectibility in its signification, since the blessed have will but no power to sin, while 'power of sinning' names both the will and its defectibility. So 'the will is a power' is simply true, but 'the power of sinning is a power' is not to be granted without distinction.
claims: 'Power of sinning' signifies the will together with its defectibility.
The blessed have will but no power to sin.
'The will is a power' is true simpliciter; 'the power to sin is a power' requires distinction.

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e227.summary: Reply to the parity argument: knowing and willing regard their objects as represented, and a privation can be represented through the likeness of the good it lacks, so knowing the privation is knowing and rejecting it is truly willing (willing it only per accidens). Power, however, regards its object according to real being, and sin's deformity has no real being, so to be able to commit it is not ability but inability.
claims: Knowledge and will relate to objects as represented; power relates to real being.
Privation can be known through the good it lacks.
Since sin's deformity has no real being, power for it is really impotence.

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e257.summary: First argument that the power to sin is not from God: whose is the power, his is the act (De somno et vigilia); sinning is not from God, so neither is the power.
claims: The source of a power is the source of its act (argument).

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e273.summary: Second argument: per Boethius, what has a good use is good and conversely; the use of the power to sin is sinning, not good, so the power is not good and not from God.
claims: A thing whose use is evil is not good (argument).

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e282.summary: Third argument: God's works are perfect (Deuteronomy 32), but the power to sin is imperfect since it names a defectibility.
claims: God's works are perfect (argument).

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e293.summary: Sed contra: Aristotle (Topics IV) says the powers of the wicked are choiceworthy, and everything choiceworthy is from God.
claims: Powers of the wicked are choiceworthy.

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e303.summary: Second sed contra: Augustine (De natura boni) says the power to harm is only from God, and that is the power to sin.
claims: The power to harm comes only from God.

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e312.summary: Richard's solution: the power of sinning is the principle both of the essence of the sinful act and of the deformity underlying it. As principle of the act's essence it is something positive and from God, and so is the act's essence. As principle of deformity it is not from God, since it names a defectibility that follows the power because it comes from nothing; that deformity has no efficient but only a deficient cause.
claims: The power to sin is from God insofar as it causes the act's positive essence.
The deformity of sin is not from God.
Defectibility follows from creation ex nihilo.
Sin's deformity has a deficient, not an efficient, cause.

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e338.summary: The arguments against divine origin hold of the power as defectible and as principle of deformity; in that respect it is true that it is not from God.

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e354.summary: The arguments for divine origin hold of the power as principle of the act's essence underlying the deformity; in that respect it is good and from God.

kzz7yh-f124277-d1e363.summary: Alternative reply to Aristotle: he may mean the powers of the wicked are choiceworthy insofar as they are the same powers that the good possess.
claims: The powers of the wicked are good as shared with the good.

kzz7yh-f124277-Dd1e115.summary: Question 1 holds that the power of sinning is a defectible power. In its essence (the will) it is a power, but in respect of its defectibility it is rather an impotence, which is why Anselm denies it is freedom or part of freedom. 'Will' does not signify defectibility, since the blessed have will without the power to sin, whereas 'power of sinning' connotes it. Hence the will is simply a power, while the power of sinning is one only with qualification. The parity with knowing and willing sin fails because knowledge and will regard objects as represented, while power regards real being, and sin's deformity has none.
claims: The power to sin is a power in essence and an impotence as defectible.
Sin's deformity has no real being.

kzz7yh-f124277-Dd1e253.summary: Question 2 holds that the power of sinning is from God in one respect and not in another. As principle of the positive essence of the act it is something positive and from God. As principle of the deformity it is not from God, since its defectibility follows from the creature's origin from nothing, and the deformity has only a deficient, not an efficient, cause. The arguments on each side are true in their respective senses.
claims: God causes the power and act of sin in their positive being but not their deformity.
Sin's deformity has a deficient cause.

kzz7yh-f124277.summary: Article 1 of II d.44 analyses the power of sinning. It is the will taken together with a defectibility: a power in its essence, but an impotence as defectible, which is why the blessed, though they have will, lack it, and why Anselm denies it belongs to freedom. That defectibility arises from the creature's origin from nothing. Richard therefore splits divine causality. The power, as principle of the positive essence of the act, is from God; the deformity of sin has no efficient cause but only a deficient one, and it is not from God.
claims: The power to sin is a defectible power, a power in essence and an impotence as defectible.
God causes the positive being of the sinful act but not its deformity.
Sin's deformity has a deficient cause rooted in creation ex nihilo.
